title: DOJ Lawsuit in Alaska Senate Race Sparks Fierce Debate Over Voter Confusion
snippet: Attorney General Todd Blanche defended a federal lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska's Senate election if GOP incumbent Dan Sullivan loses, pointing to potential confusion caused by a second candidate with the same name.
content:
In a dramatic legal escalation ahead of the midterms, the U.S. Department of Justice is seeking to prevent election officials in Alaska from certifying the state's U.S. Senate race results if Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan loses his reelection bid.

Attorney General Todd Blanche took to the Sunday news circuit to defend the lawsuit filed late last week. The Department of Justice argues that the presence of a second candidate named Dan J. Sullivan Jr. on the general election ballot creates an unconstitutional level of voter confusion. The second candidate, a lifelong Democrat who previously donated to Sullivan's Democratic challenger, former Rep. Mary Peltola, is running on the state's four-person ranked-choice ballot.

Tense Exchanges on Sunday Shows

During a contentious interview on CNN's 'State of the Union,' anchor Dana Bash pressed Blanche on what specific crime the federal government was alleging. Blanche maintained that the administration was acting to protect voters from being misled.

'There could be a crime,' Blanche said during the broadcast. 'But the real wrong here is that Alaskans are going to be confused and will not have their vote heard. So an Alaskan intends to vote for one candidate, but is confused because of a second candidate with exactly the same name who has voted Democrat his entire life.'

When asked how two individuals sharing a name on a ballot constitutes an illegal act, Blanche insisted states have an obligation under federal law and the Constitution to prevent voter confusion during federal elections. The exchange turned heated when Bash questioned whether the lawsuit was an attempt to lay groundwork to overturn election results, a premise Blanche forcefully rejected as 'embarrassing' for the network.

Blanche faced similar pushback on CBS's 'Face the Nation,' where anchor Margaret Brennan noted that Alaska officials already designated the incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan as a 'Registered Republican' and 'incumbent' on the ballot, while leaving no designation for his namesake. Blanche argued that state election officials themselves had acknowledged potential for confusion and claimed the DOJ suit merely seeks to put 'guardrails' in place to preserve ballots for review.

Local Backlash and Trump's Response

The federal intervention has drawn sharp pushback from within Alaska. The state Supreme Court previously ruled in June that both candidates could remain on the ballot, and state officials took steps to distinguish the two men on printed ballots.

Alaska Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski publicly criticized the lawsuit on social media, stating that Alaskans do not need federal intervention and that state officials had already resolved the issue. 'The Department of Justice should never have filed this lawsuit,' Murkowski wrote.

Her comments drew swift condemnation from former President Donald Trump, who took credit for initiating the legal challenge. In a post on Truth Social, Trump blasted Murkowski and slammed Alaska's ranked-choice voting system as a 'TOTAL DEMOCRAT SCAM' designed to siphon votes away from the GOP incumbent.

Concerns Over Post-Election Challenges

Democratic leaders condemned the DOJ's lawsuit as an attempt to undermine public trust in the election process. Speaking on NBC's 'Meet the Press,' Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) argued the lawsuit lacks legal standing and serves as a troubling preview of how the administration might handle contested election outcomes.

With mail-in voting already underway across Alaska, legal scholars note that proving voter confusion on secret ballots presents a massive evidentiary hurdle, making it uncertain how federal courts will address the Justice Department's demands before the final vote count.
